item.research_question: How do additive manufacturing (AM) techniques and post-heat treatments influence the microstructure, mechanical properties, and deformation mechanisms of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) compared to conventional casting methods?
item.material_system: CoCrFeNi, AlxCoCrFeNi (x=0.3, 0.6, 0.85), CoCrFeMnNi, FeCoCrAlCu, Ti25Zr50Nb0Ta25, CoCrFeNiTi, and AA5083/CoCrFeNi composites
item.processing_route: Selective Laser Melting (SLM), Laser Metal Deposition (LMD/DMD/DLF), and Selective Electron Beam Melting (SEBM); parameters include layer thickness (20–100 μm), volumetric energy density (VED), laser power (e.g., 400 W), scanning speed (e.g., 1200 mm/s), and pre-heating; post-treatments include High Isostatic Pressing (HIP) at 1100 °C for 2 h, annealing (750–1000 °C), and solution treatment.
item.test_conditions: Tensile and compression tests at room temperature (298 K) and cryogenic temperature (77 K); microstructural analysis via XRD, SEM, TEM, and EBSD; wear resistance testing.
key_findings: AM-processed HEAs exhibit superior yield strength and ductility compared to casting counterparts due to fine microstructures formed by rapid solidification.
SLM CoCrFeNi specimens showed significantly higher yield strength than arc-melt specimens while retaining significant ductility.
Increasing volumetric energy density (VED) in SLM CoCrFeMnNi reduced holes and cracks, leading to higher ultimate tensile strength.
HIP treatment at 1100 °C for 2 h removed second-phase grain-boundary phases and segregation in Al0.3CoCrFeNi, achieving chemical homogenization.
SEBM AlCoCrFeNi specimens displayed better plasticity than cast specimens due to finer grains and a substantial fraction of ductile FCC phase.
Cryogenic testing (77 K) on LAM-fabricated CrMnFeCoNi HEA enhanced yield strength and ductility, with deformation twinning becoming more obvious at high strain.
Solution treatment of SEBM CoCrFeNiTi HEA improved ductility without lowering strength by removing needle-like Ni3Ti precipitates.
Different AM methods induce substantial differences in yield strength and plasticity; for instance, DLF Al0.3CoCrFeNi showed much lower yield strength compared to SLM and SEBM methods.
item.mechanism: The enhanced mechanical properties are primarily ascribed to the refinement of microstructures caused by large temperature gradients and rapid solidification during AM, which leads to fine cellular dendrite structures, high dislocation densities, and suppressed elemental segregation. Post-treatments like HIP and annealing further enhance properties by removing fabrication defects (pores, microcracks) and releasing residual stress, while specific heat treatments can dissolve or modify precipitates (e.g., Ni3Ti, B2 phases) to optimize the balance between strength and ductility.
item.limitations: Defects such as residual stress, microcracks, and pores exist in as-built AM components, degrading mechanical properties; some AM specimens exhibit anisotropy in mechanical properties due to texture and grain orientation; limited ductility is observed in some Al-rich alloys due to brittle phase appearance; most existing studies focus on tension/compression, with rare data on fracture toughness, fatigue, oxidation, irradiation, or corrosion.
item.future_work: Optimize processing parameters and heat treatment regimes to improve microstructures and reduce residual stress; investigate fracture toughness, fatigue, oxidation, irradiation, and corrosion properties; expand research to light-weight and refractory HEAs; develop broader compositional ranges; investigate materials with large differences in melting temperatures; and study effective powder blending methods to reduce agglomeration and increase homogeneity.
quotes: Compared with the casting counterparts, AM-HEAs were found to have a superior yield strength and ductility as a consequence of the fine microstructure formed during the rapid solidification in the fabrication process.
The post-treatment, such as high isostatic pressing (HIP), can further enhance their properties by removing the existing fabrication defects and residual stress in the AM-HEAs.

The improved mechanical behavior of AM samples, compared with casting materials, is ascribed to the refinement of microstructures caused by large temperature gradients, rapid solidification, and cooling in the fabrication process.
